title: Total information from two incompatible measurements, and a proof for one form of information causality
authors: Baichu Yu, Zhang Zhou, Zhiyuan Li, Jiajun Zhang
problem: A single measurement on an ensemble of quantum states can extract at most the accessible information, which may be strictly less than the Holevo quantity \(\chi\). Two incompatible measurements, each performed on separate copies, give two label–outcome distributions but no joint distribution of their outcomes. Can a total information be defined from these two pair distributions alone, and does it stay below \(\chi\)? The question matters for information causality, where an earlier proposal measured Bob's total information across two decoding choices this way, but nobody had proved that quantum strategies respect it.
result: Using the Harder–Salge–Polani redundancy, the paper defines a total information \(R_{\rm PD}\) of two records and proves that, optimized over pairs of measurements, it lies between the accessible information and the Holevo quantity: \(I_{\rm acc}\le R_{\rm PD}\le\chi\) for every finite-dimensional classical–quantum ensemble. For the four BB84 states, measuring in the \(Z\) and \(X\) bases gives \(R_{\rm PD}=1=\chi\), while the accessible information is \(1/2\). Applied to the information-causality protocol, the upper bound proves that the redundancy-based condition holds for every quantum strategy.
significance: The redundancy-based condition had been supported only numerically. With this proof, a violation is a genuine certificate that a correlation is beyond quantum within that protocol. The key inequality is also of independent interest: whatever new posterior structure a second measurement reveals cannot exceed the information destroyed by the first.
limitations: \(R_{\rm PD}\) is defined geometrically and has no known operational meaning; the authors stress it is not information extractable from one copy. The construction covers two measurements, and a multivariate version would need a joint structure that incompatible measurements lack. A post-quantum correlation that satisfies all known forms of information causality, including this one, already exists, so satisfying the condition does not prove quantumness. The quantum-validity proof is short once the hierarchy is established; its main tool is a 2015 recovery bound of Brandão, Harrow, Oppenheim and Strelchuk. The authors state that the tool "ScienceLab AutoProject" assisted with the proof and the presentation, and in particular suggested the recovery-channel technique for the main theorem; they reviewed and verified all arguments.
summary_basis: Description based on the full arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-24: Secs. I–VI, including the definitions (Eqs. 5–17), the main theorem and its proof (Lemmas 4–5, Eqs. 42–65) and the information-causality application (Eqs. 66–70). The appendix proof of Proposition 2 was not read. Editorial checks: for the BB84 ensemble the computed values are I(A;Z) = I(A;X) = 0.5000, both directed novelties 0.5000, R = 1.0000 and chi = 1.0000. Over 150 random classical–quantum ensembles (qubits and qutrits, two to four states, pure and mixed) with random pairs of projective or general measurements, R_PD never exceeded chi; the largest value of R_PD − chi was −0.0064. The derivation of Proposition 2 from a first-order condition is editorial.

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: A label \(A\) is drawn with probability \(p_a\) and the state \(\rho_a\) is prepared. A measurement produces a record \(B\), and \(I(A;B)\) is what it reveals. The best single measurement gives the accessible information; the Holevo quantity \(\chi\) is the mutual information between the label and the unmeasured system. For BB84 states, a \(Z\) measurement learns which of \(\ket0,\ket1\) was sent when the basis was \(Z\) and nothing otherwise, and an \(X\) measurement does the reverse. Each gives half a bit, and no single measurement does better.

Two records from alternative measurements cannot be added, because they may describe the same features of the label. Partial information decomposition separates redundant and unique information, but usually starts from a joint distribution, which incompatible measurements do not provide. The Harder–Salge–Polani redundancy uses only the two pair distributions. Each outcome of a measurement yields a posterior distribution over labels, and each record generates the convex set of mixtures of its posteriors. The directed novelty \(\delta_{j\to i}\) is the average relative-entropy distance from \(B_j\)'s posteriors to the set generated by \(B_i\): the part of what \(B_j\) says that no coarse-graining of \(B_i\) could have said.

The total information is \(R_{\rm PD}=\max\{I(A;B_1)+\delta_{2\to1},\,I(A;B_2)+\delta_{1\to2}\}\), which equals the two mutual informations minus the HSP redundancy. It lies between the larger and the sum of the two informations, and it is no larger than the joint information of any coupling consistent with both pair distributions. When the two records are posterior-orthogonal, meaning their posterior deviations from the prior are orthogonal in the \(1/p(a)\)-weighted inner product, the redundancy vanishes and \(R_{\rm PD}\) is the sum. The \(Z\) and \(X\) records of BB84 are of this kind, which gives \(R_{\rm PD}=1\).

The upper bound \(R_{\rm PD}\le\chi\) follows from a directed inequality: the novelty of \(B_j\) relative to \(B_i\) is at most \(\chi-I(A;B_i)\), the information that measurement \(i\) destroys. In the information-causality game Alice holds \(A\), sends a message of capacity \(k\), and Bob chooses one of two decodings of his share of a no-signalling resource. For quantum resources Bob's system before the message carries no information about \(A\), so \(\chi\le k\), and the hierarchy gives \(IC_{\rm red}\le k\) for every quantum strategy.

methods.technique: Directed posterior novelty as a relative-entropy projection
methods.explanation: Each outcome of a measurement updates the prior to a posterior. Whatever another record can learn by post-processing this one lies in the convex hull of these posteriors. The new content of a second record is the distance from its posteriors to that hull.
math: Let \(\mathcal C_i=\mathrm{conv}\{p_i(A|b_i)\}\). The directed novelty and the total information are \[\delta_{j\to i}=\sum_{b_j}p_j(b_j)\inf_{r\in\mathcal C_i}D\bigl(p_j(A|b_j)\,\|\,r\bigr),\qquad R_{\rm PD}=\max_{i\ne j}\bigl\{I(A;B_i)+\delta_{j\to i}\bigr\}.\] Since the prior \(p(A)\) is the average of \(B_i\)'s posteriors, it lies in \(\mathcal C_i\), and the infimum is at most \(D(p_j(A|b_j)\|p(A))\). Averaging gives \(\delta_{j\to i}\le I(A;B_j)\).

Editorial derivation of the orthogonal case. \(D(P\|r)\) is convex in \(r\), so \(p(A)\) minimizes it over \(\mathcal C_i\) if no direction into \(\mathcal C_i\) decreases it to first order. Moving from \(p\) towards a posterior \(q\) of \(B_i\), the derivative in natural units is \[-\sum_a\frac{P(a)\,[q(a)-p(a)]}{p(a)}=-\sum_a\frac{[P(a)-p(a)][q(a)-p(a)]}{p(a)},\] because \(\sum_a[q(a)-p(a)]=0\). Posterior orthogonality makes this zero for every posterior \(q\), and hence for every point of \(\mathcal C_i\). So the projection is the prior, \(\delta_{j\to i}=I(A;B_j)\), and \(R_{\rm PD}=I(A;B_1)+I(A;B_2)\).

For BB84 with uniform prior, a \(Z\) outcome gives posterior \((\tfrac12,0,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)\) or \((0,\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)\) over \((0,1,+,-)\), and an \(X\) outcome gives \((\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac12,0)\) or \((\tfrac14,\tfrac14,0,\tfrac12)\). The deviations from the uniform prior are \((\tfrac14,-\tfrac14,0,0)\)-type and \((0,0,\tfrac14,-\tfrac14)\)-type vectors, which are orthogonal. Each record carries \(\tfrac12\) bit, so \(R_{\rm PD}=1\).
methods.transfer: Relative-entropy projection onto the hull of one experiment's posteriors measures what a second experiment adds without needing a joint distribution. It applies to comparing incompatible detectors, sensors or tomographic settings run on separate samples.

methods.technique: Novelty bounded by measurement loss through a recovery map
methods.explanation: The information destroyed by a measurement is a conditional mutual information in its Stinespring dilation. A recovery theorem converts small conditional mutual information into a good recovery map, and any statistics produced after recovery are a coarse-graining of the first record.
math: Dilate measurement \(i\) by an isometry \(V_i:H\to B_iE_i\). Isometric invariance and the chain rule give \[\chi-I(A;B_i)=I(A:B_iE_i)-I(A:B_i)=I(A:E_i\,|\,B_i).\] The Brandão–Harrow–Oppenheim–Strelchuk bound states \(I(A:C|B)\ge\inf_{\mathcal R}D_{\mathrm M}\bigl(\omega_{ABC}\,\|\,\mathcal R(\omega_{AB})\bigr)\), with \(D_{\mathrm M}\) the measured relative entropy, so some recovery \(\mathcal R_i:B_i\to B_iE_i\) has error at most \(\chi-I(A;B_i)+\varepsilon\).

Map the recovered system back to \(H\) with a channel that inverts \(V_i\) on its range, then perform measurement \(j\). On the true state this produces \(p_j(A,B_j)\). On the recovered state it produces \(q(a,b_j)=\sum_{b_i}p_i(a,b_i)K(b_j|b_i)\) for a stochastic matrix \(K\), because the recovered state depends on \(B_i\) alone. Each posterior \(q(A|b_j)\) is then a mixture of \(B_i\)'s posteriors, so it lies in \(\mathcal C_i\). Data processing and the chain rule give \[D_{\mathrm M}\ge D\bigl(p_j(A,B_j)\|q(A,B_j)\bigr)\ge\sum_{b_j}p_j(b_j)\,D\bigl(p_j(A|b_j)\|q(A|b_j)\bigr)\ge\delta_{j\to i}.\]

Combining, \(I(A;B_i)+\delta_{j\to i}\le\chi\) for both orderings, hence \(R_{\rm PD}\le\chi\). In the information-causality game, Bob's precommunication system \(H\) is independent of \(A\), so \(\chi=I(A:HM)\le I(A:H)+k=k\) for a classical message of capacity \(k\). Any two decoding measurements on \(HM\) therefore give \(IC_{\rm red}=R_{\rm PD}(A;B_1,B_2)\le k\). Editorial check: random ensembles and measurement pairs never violated \(R_{\rm PD}\le\chi\) numerically.
methods.transfer: Rewriting a loss of mutual information as a conditional mutual information and invoking a recovery theorem is a general way to show that a quantity defined by post-processing cannot exceed what was lost. It applies to bounds on residual or destroyed information after measurement and to sequential measurement schemes.
